chunks.text:
About this Class
Administrative Stuff
The UE Project
Introduction to Classiﬁcation
Preview
Literature
About this Class
What this class is:
▶The ﬁrst machine learning class ever offered at JKU
▶Mandatory for AI Bachelor’s students (4th →2nd semester)
▶A basic introduction to supervised machine learning for classiﬁcation tasks
▶with a very strong focus on what it means to do machine learning in the “real
world”.
▶To this end: focus on a complex practical project (UE) ...
▶.. and in class, learn what you need to know in order to carry out such a
project, and learn something from it.
What this class is not:
▶a specialised class on neural networks and ‘deep learning’
▶an advanced class on current methods of statistical learning.
There are lots of specialised (and good) ML courses at JKU, focusing on
neural networks, ‘deep learning’, reinforcement learning, etc.
Who this class is for:
▶anyone interested in the fundamentals of supervised machine learning
▶a mixed audience (CS, AI, ELIT, mechatronics, guest students)
▶(with apologies to AI students for redundancies in curriculum)

chunks.text:
About this Class
Administrative Stuff
The UE Project
Introduction to Classiﬁcation
Preview
Literature
The Institute of Computational Perception (CP.JKU)
From our Homepage:
[...] We develop and study computational models and algorithms that allow computers to
perceive and ’understand’ aspects in the external world, where we interpret ’perception’ in
the widest sense of the word as extracting useful, high-level information and knowledge
from complex, possibly low-level data (audio, video, image, text, sensor data, and user-item
interaction data). That requires fundamental and applied research in AI, machine learning,
pattern recognition, text / data / social media mining, signal processing, statistical data
modeling, and classiﬁcation.
Our current research focuses particularly on intelligent audio and music processing. We are
among the leading research groups worldwide in the ﬁelds of Music Information Research
(MIR), Sound and Music Computing (SMC), and Acoustic Scene & Event Recognition
(DCASE). Additional research topics include image processing, biometrics, cryptography,
and personalization.
For more information about our institute, see
▶www.jku.at/en/institute-of-computational-perception

chunks.text:
About this Class
Administrative Stuff
The UE Project
Introduction to Classiﬁcation
Preview
Literature
The Associated Exercise Class (UE)
This is the most instructive (and fun) part of the whole enterprise.
Teachers (SS 2026):
▶Florian Schmid, Paul Primus, Tara Jadidi, Katharina Hoedt, Tobias Morocutti,
Carlos Cancino Chac´on, Alexander Fichtinger + student tutors
Purpose:
▶For you to learn that machine learning in real problems is much more than
just applying some ML algorithm to some data
▶To gain experience with all steps in a machine learning project:
data acquisition, labeling, cleaning; preliminary data analysis; setup of
experiments; training and optimising different classiﬁers; systematic
evaluation and model selection; post-processing and optimisation.
Important Points:
▶AI Curriculum lists UE in 4th semester; but: take it now!
▶Detailed explanation of the UE Project: ﬁrst UE meeting (today, 13:45, HS 7)
▶Project will be done in groups of 2 persons
▶Please direct UE-related questions to my colleagues, not to me!

chunks.title: ▶Optional:2 Design algorithms that extract informative features from the
chunks.text:
About this Class
Administrative Stuff
The UE Project
Introduction to Classiﬁcation
Preview
Literature
Building a Classiﬁer via Machine Learning
General Approach to Decision Problem:
▶Collect a set of training examples of ﬁsh of both species
▶Have them labelled (i.e., true class determined) by ﬁsh experts
▶Set up a camera and take images of the training ﬁsh
▶Optional:2 Design algorithms that extract informative features from the
images (e.g., length, lightness, width, number and shape of ﬁns, etc.)
▶Build a classiﬁer (= decision function) from the training examples
(Classiﬁer makes decision based on features only)
▶Test reliability of classiﬁer experimentally
▶If found to be reliable enough, use classiﬁer in real application context.
2Some models (e.g., Deep Neural Networks) can also learn features as part of the process

chunks.title: ▶Reduce and abstract the data (pixel images) by identifying and measuring
chunks.text:
About this Class
Administrative Stuff
The UE Project
Introduction to Classiﬁcation
Preview
Literature
Classiﬁcation: Main Processing Steps
Preprocessing:
▶Use a segmentation algorithm to isolate ﬁsh from one another in the image,
and from the background (image processing)
Feature Extraction:
▶Reduce and abstract the data (pixel images) by identifying and measuring
certain features (characteristics)
Classiﬁcation:
▶Pass the features to a classiﬁer that decides on the category of the ﬁsh
▶Usually, such classiﬁers will not be built manually, but trained (learned by the
computer from example data)
 Importance of Machine Learning (sub-ﬁeld of AI and statistics)
14 / 30

Beyond Perfect Discrimination on the Training Data
Consider this:

▶... to correctly classify new, unseen cases
⇒Importance of Generalisation
Questions:
▶Do the few errors (and the small number of training examples) really justify
this complex decision boundary?
▶Is it really plausible that the true underlying concept (nature) is so complex?
▶Maybe some of the odd examples are rare/unusual outliers, or the result of
measurement errors, or have incorrect class labels?

Probabilities and Densities
Probability Distributions vs. Density Functions
The discrete case:
▶For a discrete variable X with a ﬁnite set of values Val(X) = {x1, ..., xn}, a
Probability Distribution or Probability Mass Function assigns a
probability P(xi) to each value xi
▶Example: a biased coin C with values Val(C) = {heads, tails} might have
P(heads) = 0.35;
P(tails) = 0.65
▶Over all values, the distribution must sum to 1: P(heads) + P(tails) = 1.0
Deﬁnition
A Probability Distribution over a discrete variable X = {x1, ..., xn} is a
function P : X 7→[0, 1] ⊂R+ with P
i P(xi) = 1.0
The Joint Distribution over a set of d discrete variables {X1, ..., Xd} is a
function P : X1 × ... × Xd 7→[0, 1] that assigns a probability to each possible
combination of values of the variables
 A distribution can be thought of as a list of n numbers.
A joint distribution is a d-dimensional table with nd entries.

The Reverend Thomas Bayes
Quote from the Encyclopedia Britannica (quote and image taken from the International
Society for Bayesian Analysis [http://bayesian.org/bayes]):
Bayes, Thomas (b. 1702, London - d. 1761, Tunbridge Wells, Kent), mathematician who
ﬁrst used probability inductively and established a mathematical basis for probability
inference (a means of calculating, from the number of times an event has or has not
occurred, the probability that it will occur in future trials).
He set down his ﬁndings on probability in “Essay Towards Solving a Problem in the Doctrine
of Chances” (1763), published posthumously in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal
Society of London.
The only works he is known to have published in his lifetime are “Divine Benevolence, or an
Attempt to Prove That the Principal End of the Divine Providence and Government is the
Happiness of His Creatures” (1731) and “An Introduction to the Doctrine of Fluxions, and a
Defence of the Mathematicians Against the Objections of the Author of the Analyst” (1736)
which countered attacks by Bishop Berkeley on the logical foundations of Newton’s calculus.

Generalisation of the preceding ideas:
▶Permit more than two classes
▶Permit arbitrary decisions/actions (not only to predict a certain class)
▶Introduce a loss function that speciﬁes costs of decisions (actions)
depending on true class
Remarks:
▶Allowing actions other than class predictions primarily permits the possibility
of rejection (saying “I don’t know”, e.g., in close or risky cases)
▶The loss function permits us to distinguish between different kinds of errors.

salmon may be higher than misclassifying salmon as sea bass)

Some general questions about MAP (maximum a posteriori) classiﬁcation via Bayes rule
(no cost function, no conditional risk, just predict class with maximum posterior). Which of
the following sentences are correct, which are wrong?
▶The posterior can never be exactly 1.0
▶The posterior can never be exactly 0.0
▶The posterior can never be larger than the prior
▶The posterior can never be larger than the likelihood
▶If we have a prior that puts a probability of 1.0 on one class and 0.0 on all others, the
classiﬁer can never predict any of these other classes
▶The likelihood expresses the probability that a certain feature combination will appear
in examples of a given class
▶The likelihood expresses the probability that examples with a certain feature
combination will belong to a particular class
▶If we have a uniform prior (i.e., one that assigns the same probability to each class),
then the posterior will also give the same probability to each class, for a given input
vector x
▶If we have a uniform prior (i.e., one that assigns the same probability to each class),
then arg maxi P(ωi | x) = arg maxi p(x | ωi)
▶A posterior probability P(ωi | x) < 0 means that the class ωi does not exist
▶A posterior probability P(ωi | x) = 0 means that x cannot belong to class ωi

chunks.title: ▶Prior probability distribution P(Ω) over classes: what is the probability
chunks.text:
Motivation
Parametric Density Estimation
Non-parametric Density Estimation
From Density Estimation to NN Classiﬁers
Literature
Learning Probabilities from Data
Obvious Solution:
▶Try to estimate true probabilities from given training examples
 ‘Learning’
▶In many cases, training examples are our only source of information
Need to learn:
▶Prior probability distribution P(Ω) over classes: what is the probability
P(ωi) that a randomly drawn example would belong to class ωi?
▶Class-conditional probability distributions / density functions p(X | Ω):
for each class ωi, what is the probability, for each possible observation
(combination of feature values) x ∈X, that an example randomly drawn
from class ωi would display the speciﬁc feature combination x?
(⇒need joint distribution over d-dimensional feature space!)
Problems:
▶Huge or inﬁnite feature space (set of possible value combinations) X!
▶Limited information in limited set of training examples
▶How to specify (possibly high-dimensional joint) probability distributions?

chunks.title: 2. Non-parametric Density Estimation:
chunks.text:
Motivation
Parametric Density Estimation
Non-parametric Density Estimation
From Density Estimation to NN Classiﬁers
Literature
Learning Probabilities from Data
Two Families of Methods:
1. Parametric Density Estimation:
▶Assume the observations are generated by a speciﬁc family of distributions
that can be described with a ﬁnite set of parameters
▶Try to estimate these parameters from the training set D
2. Non-parametric Density Estimation:
▶Place no constraint on the shape of the underlying distribution p
▶p could have any ‘shape’
▶Do not attempt to describe the full distribution over the entire feature space
▶Instead: try to estimate the probability density p(x | ωi) for a given feature
combination x locally, on demand (when needed for classiﬁcation)

chunks.text:
Motivation
Parametric Density Estimation
Non-parametric Density Estimation
From Density Estimation to NN Classiﬁers
Literature
Parameter Estimation: Two Fundamental Approaches
1. Maximum Likelihood Estimation:
▶View parameters θ as quantities with ﬁxed but unknown values
▶Best estimate ˆθ is the one that gives a distribution that best ‘agrees with’ the
observed data D
▶‘Agreement’ with the data is deﬁned via the likelihood L(θ : D) (next slide)
▶Result of estimation is one speciﬁc set of parameter values ˆθ
2. Bayesian Parameter Estimation:
▶View parameters themselves as random variables with some prior
distribution p(θ)
▶In other words: consider all possible parameter settings, with different
probabilities
▶Result of estimation is a posterior probability distribution over
parametrisations, given the data:
p(θ | D) = P(D | θ)p(θ)
P(D)
▶Not treated here. See my class “Probabilistic Models” in the WS.

Motivation

From Density Estimation to NN Classiﬁers
Literature
Maximum Likelihood Parameter Estimation
Task:
▶Given: a set of training observations D = {x1, ..., xn}
▶Assumption: a certain family of distributions underlying the data,
parametrisable via set of parameters θ
▶Task: Find values ˆθ that have the highest likelihood in view of the given
data D
Deﬁnition
The Likelihood of a set of parameters θ relative to a set of observations D is the
probability that a distribution with these parameters would give to the
observations:
L(θ : D) = p(D | θ)
In Words: the Likelihood is ...
▶the probability that one would get exactly the instances in D if one randomly
drew n = |D| samples from the distribution pθ(X)
▶the degree to which pθ(X) “explains” the observations D.

Motivation
Parametric Density Estimation
Non-parametric Density Estimation
From Density Estimation to NN Classiﬁers
Literature
Our First Learning Algorithms: Single-Gaussian Classiﬁer and Na¨ıve Bayes
The Na¨ıve Bayes Classiﬁer
Problems with the algorithm:
▶”Na¨ıve”: the independence assumption is often extremely wrong
▶It says: there are no correlations at all between features within a class
▶If not true ⇒get incorrect probability estimates
▶Limited expressive/discriminative power: can only model relatively simple
decision boundaries (disregards feature interactions)
Advantages:

chunks.text:
Motivation
Parametric Density Estimation
Non-parametric Density Estimation
From Density Estimation to NN Classiﬁers
Literature
Approach 2: Non-parametric Density Estimation
Recap so far:
▶In parametric estimation, we assumed that the shape (family) of
probability/density function is known
▶Problem was just to estimate the parameters of this function
Problems:
▶Common parametric shapes rarely ﬁt densities encountered in real data
▶In particular: all the ‘classical’ families of parametric density functions (e.g.,
the Gaussian) are unimodal (have a single maximum), while many practical
problems (data) involve multimodal densities!
(Example: there might be two different subspecies of salmon – large light
ones and smaller dark ones ⇒two ‘clouds’ of points in feature space)
Possible way out: Nonparametric Estimation
▶Make no assumption about the underlying distribution p: could be any shape
▶Do not attempt to describe the full distribution over the entire feature space
▶Instead: estimate probability/density p(x|ωi) for a given instance x locally,
on demand (when needed for classiﬁcation)

A Generalisation of NN Density Estimation:
Estimation via Kernel Functions
Basic Idea:
▶View each training instance xi as generating a little density function (a
kernel function) K(xi, ·) of its own
▶Kernel function is centered on xi and decays with distance from xi
▶Density estimate over entire space is just the normalised sum of the little
kernel functions
▶Density estimate at a point x is P
xi∈D K(xi, x)
Motivation:
▶All training examples contribute to density estimate everywhere
▶Instead of counting (as in NN estimation), contribution of xi to estimate p(x)
is weighted by a function K of its distance to x
▶Expected effect: smoother estimates than with NN estimation

chunks.title: ▶But: number of training examples needed to guarantee a certain ﬁxed
chunks.text:
Motivation
Parametric Density Estimation
Non-parametric Density Estimation
From Density Estimation to NN Classiﬁers
Literature
The Curse of Dimensionality
The “Curse of Dimensionality”
Problem:
▶Quality of class prediction depends on ‘density’ of training instances around
query point x (there should be a sufﬁcient number of similar cases to make
a justiﬁed prediction)
▶But: number of training examples needed to guarantee a certain ﬁxed
density everywhere in feature space (on average) grows exponentially with
number of dimensions d
▶Or conversely: High-dimensional spaces are extremely sparsely populated
by a given (ﬁxed-size) training set D
⇒Nearest neighbours in high-dimensional spaces are usually far away from x
(i.e., very different)!
Another way of looking at it:
▶With large number of features, most features may be irrelevant to the class
▶Distance measure is unaware of this, considers all features equally
▶Consequence: distance is dominated by irrelevant (“random”) information,
relevant similarities/differences are obscured
⇒Need for feature selection
The problem affects all distance-/neighbour-based methods for prediction.

of d features

▶The world X is governed by a ﬁxed (but unknown) probability
distribution p(X, Ω) over features and classes
▶As training data, we obtain a set D of example cases that have been drawn
from this world according to the underlying distribution p

by some external expert entity.
▶The training examples have been drawn independently and all come from
the same distribution p1
▶The distribution p(X, Ω) will not change over time (or between training and
application time) – it is stationary

Evaluation Measures

Literature
Evaluating Classiﬁers
Central Question:
▶How good is a classiﬁer c learned from D by algorithm L?
▶Criterion: should predict correct classes on new, unseen cases in the future
▶For the moment, assume we want a classiﬁer with low prediction error
(see later slides for alternative evaluation criteria)
Deﬁnition
The (True) Error Ep(c) of a classiﬁer c is the probability that c will predict the
wrong class for an instance x randomly drawn from world (feature space) X
according to the underlying distribution p(X) (or, in other words, the probability of
drawing an instance x from X for which c will predict the wrong class):
Ep(c) = P(x ∈X : c(x) ̸= class(x))

Accuracy Estimation (3): k-fold Cross-Validation
Cross-Validation Estimate: Procedure
▶Randomly split D into k subsets (‘folds’) F1, ..., Fk of approx. equal size
▶For i = 1...k : Learn classiﬁer ci from set D \ Fi
▶Test ci on test set Fi (which was not used in training)

▶Leave-one-out cross-validation: k = number of examples |D| (i.e., each
example in D is its own fold). Useful when little data available.

chunks.text:
The General Setting
Empirical Evaluation of Classiﬁers
Overﬁtting & Model Selection
Evaluation Measures
Cost-sensitive Learning
Literature
Bias vs. Variance
Bias
Goal:
▶Avoid learning an overﬁtting model
▶Force learner to generalise
Approach:
▶Put constraints on models (decision boundaries) allowed to the learner:
▶Hard constraints: Strictly restrict the class C of models (e.g., only permit
linear boundaries, restrict set of features to be used, etc.)
▶Soft constraints: Add a model complexity penalty to the criterion that the
learning algorithm is trying to optimise (‘Regularisation’)
Consequence:
▶Constrained models are limited in what they can represent
▶May not be able to correctly represent true decision boundaries in world X.
Error possibility introduced by restricting expressivity of model class
is called Bias.

chunks.text:
The General Setting

Overﬁtting & Model Selection
Evaluation Measures
Cost-sensitive Learning
Literature
Model Selection
The “Optimiser’s Curse”
“If you expect the accuracy of your best model to be the same as the accuracy
estimate based on which the selection was made, you will almost always be
disappointed.”
... or in more direct words:
“The validation score that led you to choose your best model is almost certainly
an overestimate of how it will perform on new data.”
▶Any accuracy estimate ˆAV (c) of a classiﬁer c obtained on a test/val set V of
ﬁnite size will have some random estimation error ϵ: ˆAV (c) = Ap(c) + ϵ
(where Ap(c) = true accuracy of c relative to the underlying distribution p)
▶When you evaluate several classiﬁers, the estimates will have different
random errors ϵ (some positive, some possibly negative)
▶Even if the estimation process is unbiased (ϵ is symmetrically distributed
around 0), picking the model with the highest ˆAV (c) will favour models with
a high ϵ, i.e., models where the accuracy was over-estimated.

Evaluation (4): ROC Analysis
Question:
▶Given two classiﬁers with same accuracy (80%) on a given dataset,
▶will they be equally good in a real application?
Example:
▶C1 correctly classiﬁes 40 out of 50 positives and 40 out of 50 negatives
▶C2 correctly classiﬁes 30 out of 50 positives and 50 out of 50 negatives
⇒both have the same test set accuracy of 80%, but:
▶in a world that has more negatives than positives (or where correct
recognition of negatives is more important), C2 will be preferable
▶in a world with more positives, C1 will be preferable
... unless the proportion of positives is so high that an ‘always positive’
predictor would be better!
 ROC Analysis is a general method for comparing classiﬁers under different
class distribution and cost scenarios

chunks.title: Notes:
chunks.text:
The General Setting
Empirical Evaluation of Classiﬁers
Overﬁtting & Model Selection
Evaluation Measures
Cost-sensitive Learning
Literature
ROC Space and ROC Analysis
The ROC Convex Hull
Deﬁnition
The ROC Convex Hull of a set of classiﬁers is the convex hull of the classiﬁers’
positions in ROC space (including the baseline classiﬁers (0, 0) and (1, 1)).
Notes:
▶The convex hull connects the best classiﬁers
▶Note: this also includes the ‘all pos’ (1,1) and ‘all neg’ (0,0) corner classiﬁers!
▶It is convex (if all classiﬁers are below the diagonal, the hull is the diagonal)
▶It can be computed in O(n log n) time
▶Any classiﬁer below the hull is suboptimal under all possible conditions
because:
▶Any desired point on the hull (i.e., a classiﬁer that has those TPR : FPR
properties) can be obtained by probabilistic combination of two
neighbouring classiﬁers

Literature
Cost-sensitive Learning: Five Simple Strategies
Over-/Undersampling:
▶Oversampling: duplicate instances of critical classes in D
▶Undersampling: remove instances to achieve desired class distribution
Instance Weighting:
▶Attach weights to individual training examples to reﬂect error cost
▶Works with learners that can handle instance weights
Modifying the Prior:
▶Set the prior class distribution to simulate the cost scenario
▶Possible with Bayesian classiﬁers
Thresholding:
▶Change the threshold that your classiﬁer uses for making the class prediction
▶Possible with classiﬁers that predict a numeric value (probability)
(e.g., Bayes, Logistic Regression, Neural Networks)
Changing the Objective Function:
▶Change the function the learner is trying to minimise on the training data
▶Possible with, e.g., neural networks, which are trained by minimising a given
error (‘loss’) function

Ockham’s Principle (“Occam’s Razor”):
“Non sunt multiplicanda entia praeter necessitatem.”
(Entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity.)
William of Ockham (1287? – 1347?)
General Interpretation of Occam’s Razor in Science:
“Among the theories consistent with observed phenomena, one
should prefer the simplest theory (all other things being equal).”
Not to be confused with Newton’s (stronger) statement:
“Natura enim simplex est, et rerum causis superﬂuis non luxuriat.”
(For nature is simple, and does not afford the pomp of superﬂuous causes.)
Isaac Newton, Preface to “Principia”a

chunks.text:
Recap: Simple ‘Baseline’ Classiﬁers
Other Popular Classiﬁers
Literature
A Classic: Decision Trees and the ID3 Algorithm
The ID3 Algorithm for Learning Decision Trees4
Basic Ideas / Properties:
▶Recursive algorithm: generate decision tree step by step, starting with the
empty tree
▶Heuristic algorithm: aim at obtaining a simple tree by heuristically choosing
features to use for splitting at tree nodes
▶Greedy algorithm: at each step, take decision (select feature) that
maximises a local optimality criterion.
Consequences:
▶Non-optimal: cannot guarantee ﬁnding the simplest possible tree
▶Short-sighted: blind to features that are predictive only in combination
(because heuristic evaluates features only individually)
▶... but efﬁcient (fast)
4Iterative Dichotomizer (Quinlan, 1986).

chunks.text:
Recap: Simple ‘Baseline’ Classiﬁers

Literature
A Classic: Decision Trees and the ID3 Algorithm
The ID3 Algorithm for Learning Decision Trees
Schema of the ID3 Algorithm
Start with root node containing all training examples: DRoot = D
ID3:
1 If all examples DN in current node N belong to the same class ω
⇒make current node a leaf, label with class ω, and EXIT
2 If no more features available for splitting in current node N a
⇒make current node a leaf, label with majority class in N, and EXIT
3 Select “best” feature AN to split instance set DN
4 Create a branch + successor node Ni for each possible value vi ∈Val(AN)
5 Split training examples DN into subsets according to their value for feature
AN; assign each subset to its respective branch/subnode
6 For each subnode: recursively call ID3
aonly in discrete-feature domains
Central Question: What is the “best” feature to split on?

The ID3 Algorithm
Start with root node containing all training examples: DRoot = D
ID3:
1 If all examples DN in current node N belong to the same class ω
⇒make current node a leaf, label with class ω, and EXIT
2 If no more features available for splitting in current node N
⇒make current node a leaf, label with majority class in N, and EXIT
3 Calculate IGDN (Ai) for all features Ai
(i.e., try out all features for splitting)
4 Select feature A = arg max
Ai IG(Ai) with max information gain (if > 0)
5 Create a branch + successor node Ni for each value vi ∈Val(A)
6 Split training examples DN into subsets according to their value for feature
A; assign each subset to its respective branch/subnode
7 For each subnode: recursively call ID3

Reduced Error Pruning (REP)
1 Randomly split training examples D into a Training Set Dtrain and a
Pruning (Validation) Set Dval
2 Learn a (possibly complex) tree T from Dtrain with minimum error
(i.e., one that possibly overﬁts on Dtrain )
3 Iteratively simplify the tree, step by step:
- for each subtree Ti of T , tentatively replace Ti by a leaf (with majority
class) and test/compare accuracy on validation set Dval
- if there is no Ti that improves accuracy when removed: EXIT
- otherwise: choose Ti with maximum improvement and replace with leaf
4 Go to 3.

increase in bias) by combining several high-variance (overﬁtting) models

(i.e., make their prediction errors on different examples)!
Central Question:

Recap: Simple ‘Baseline’ Classiﬁers
Other Popular Classiﬁers
Literature
Robustness via Linear Classiﬁcation in High-dimensional Spaces: Support Vector Machines
Simpliﬁed Scenario: Linear Separation in Original Space
▶Given: Feature space X deﬁned by a set of d features X = {X1, ..., Xd}
▶Given: Training set D = {(xi, yi)} with xi ∈X and yi ∈Ω= {−1, +1}10
▶Find: A (hyper)plane in feature space X that separates the two classes
Linear Classiﬁer:
▶Hyperplane = linear function of the features: all points that satisfy
w · x + b = 0
for some vector of coefﬁcients (weights) w ∈Rd and some offset b ∈R
▶w · x = wT x is the dot (inner, scalar) product
▶w is a normal vector to the plane
▶The hyperplane is used as a classiﬁer (linear discriminant function):
ˆy(x) = sgn(w · x + b)
In Words: The class label ˆy predicted for an example vector x is the sign (+1 or −1) of
the output of the linear function for x. (Examples x directly on the plane produce 0)
10SVMs are limited to binary classiﬁcation problems; we encode the two classes as −1 and +1

Support Vector Machines: Pros and Cons
Advantages:
▶Can approximate complex decision boundaries (low bias)
▶Robust against overﬁtting and noise in the data
⇒strike a compromise between bias and variance12
▶Can be used in very high-dimensional classiﬁcation problems (e.g.,
document classiﬁcation)
Disadvantages:
▶No interpretable model
▶Only directly applicable to 2-class problems
▶Relatively slow in training ⇒problematic for huge datasets
▶Cannot learn incrementally
12... but whether it’s the right compromise depends on whether your chosen kernel function matches
the structure of your task and data. There’s no magical solution to the bias-variance tradeoff problem ...

What to expect in the exam: A few typical questions ...
Consider a set D of training examples, described in terms of N numeric features f1, ..., fN .
Assume we create a new training set D1 from D by duplicating one of these features, fi,
10 times; in other words: by adding 10 new features fN+1, ..., fN+10 to the data that are
all identical to fi. (That is, we change the data set, not by adding new objects, but by
adding 10 copies of a feature to the description of each object.)
When we replace the training set D by the new training set D1, which of the following
learning algorithms may be affected by this feature duplication (in terms of learning a
classiﬁer that now predicts differently):
▶k-NN with k = 1 and Euclidean distance
▶k-NN with k > 1 and Euclidean distance
▶Standard Decision Tree Learner (ID3)
▶A restricted version of ID3 that can only learn “decision stumps” (i.e., a one-level tree
with a feature at the root and leaves below that)
▶Na¨ıve Bayes
▶A feed-forward neural network without hidden layer (i.e., logistic regression)
▶A Support Vector Machine with the Quadratic Kernel as explained in the lecture slides
▶A maximum margin linear classiﬁer using only the given features

Ensemble Methods (4): Boosting (Freund & Shapire, 1996)
Basic Idea:
▶Generate a series of N classiﬁers ci with a given learning algorithm
▶... from a series of training sets Dt with differently weighted examples
▶Examples get higher weight in Dt+1 if classiﬁer ct got them wrong
⇒Forces next classiﬁer ct+1 to focus on weaknesses of ct
Boosting: The General Algorithm Schema
Initialise: Let D1 = D with uniform weights
For t = 1...N do:
▶Learn classiﬁer ct from weighted training seta Dt
▶Compute ct’s error ϵt on its training set Dt
▶Create data set Dt+1 by reweighting examples in Dt:
increase weight if example was misclassiﬁed by ct, decrease otherwise
Classiﬁcation of new object x:
▶Weighted majority vote of all N classiﬁers
▶Weight each classiﬁer ct with its accuracy on its respective training set Dt

chunks.title: ▶Slide window over sequence of predicted class labels
chunks.text:

Literature
Post-Processing (1): Smoothing Prediction Sequences
Basic Idea:
▶If a single audio frame x is classiﬁed as “no music”, and all or most of its
surrounding frames are labeled as “music”, then x is very likely misclassiﬁed
and should be re-labeled as “music” (and vice versa)
Method:
▶Slide window over sequence of predicted class labels
▶For each frame x, look at N frames surrounding x
▶Let these neighbours “vote” on the class of x: assign most frequent class in
window to x
▶Labels change from left to right ⇒repeat the procedure
Window Functions:
▶unweighted (vote by majority)
▶distance-weighted voting (e.g., via
pseudo-Gaussian weighting function)

Artiﬁcial Neural Networks (ANNs)

▶Distributed computation model based on interconnected units (“neurons”)
▶Originally motivated by analogies to information processing in the brain:
- Neurons connected by dendrites and synapses
- Neurons “ﬁre” (send out an output signal) when input exceeds a threshold
▶First fundamental aspects of biological neurons studied and modelled
already in the 1940’s
▶First simple (two-level) artiﬁcial neural networks (“Perceptrons”) formalised
and simulated in the 1960’s
▶1980’s: Backpropagation Algorithm for training networks with hidden layers

chunks.title: General Algorithm for Approximate Solution: Iterative Gradient Descent
chunks.text:
Artiﬁcial Neural Networks (ANNs)
Feed-Forward Networks (Multi-layer Perceptrons, MLPs)
MLPs for Classiﬁcation
Literature
A Gentle Introduction: The Regression Task
Parameter Optimisation via Gradient Descent
Goal:
▶Find model parameters θ = {w1, w0} that minimise loss E on training set D
▶For linear models, solution can be calculated analytically
(Least Squares Linear Regression)
▶But: not possible for general non-linear models (see later)
General Algorithm for Approximate Solution: Iterative Gradient Descent
Iterative Gradient Descent
1 Choose some (random) initial values for model parameters θ
2 Observe error E of resulting model on training data D
3 Calculate gradient Gθi of error function E w.r.t each parameter θi ∈θ
4 Change parameters slightly – moderated by a factor η (learning rate) – so
that we move a bit in the direction of the greatest rate of decrease of the
error, i.e., in the direction of −G:
θi ←(θi −η · Gθi)
5 Repeat steps 2 to 4 until G gets (close to) zero.

Deﬁnition
A Multi-layer Feed-forward Network (Multi-layer Perceptron) is a network
composed of the following parts:
▶an input layer of n units coding the inputs to the network
▶h ≥1 hidden layers L1, ..., Lh consisting of mi units, respectively
▶an output layer of m units, to code (possibly multiple) outputs
▶Connections: all units of a layer are connected to all units of the next layer.
Usual (‘classical’) conﬁguration:
▶Only one hidden layer (sufﬁcient for
universal function approximation)
▶Input values in range (e.g., [−1, 1])
▶Only units in hidden layer(s) use a
non-linear activation function f
▶Input and output units use the trivial
identity function f(x) = x

degree of accuracy

Feed-forward ANNs in Concise Matrix Notation
Concise Mathematical Summary of Feed-Forward Networks
A Neuron y is a (non-linear) transformation of a linear sum of its inputs x:
y = f(wT x + b)
where
x = [x1, ..., xn]T is a vector of incoming values
w = [w1, ..., wn]T is a vector of weights
b is the weight from the bias unit
f is an activation function
A Layer is an array (vector) of neurons y = [y1, ..., ym]T :
y = f(W T x + b)
where
x = [x1, ..., xn]T is a vector of incoming values
W = [w1, ..., wm] is an n × m weight matrix (set of m column vectors)
b = [b1, ..., bm] is a vector of bias weights.
Function f is applied point-wise to each element of its argument vector

chunks.text:
Artiﬁcial Neural Networks (ANNs)
Feed-Forward Networks (Multi-layer Perceptrons, MLPs)
MLPs for Classiﬁcation
Literature
Training MLPs: Gradient Descent and Error-Backpropagation
Training a Multi-layer Network
Learning Task:
▶Given dataset D = {(xi, yi)} of training examples with input values xi and
(numeric) target values yi
▶Learn (ﬁnd) values for the network’s parameters θ = {Wl, bl}
(i.e., values for all the weights in the network)
▶such that a given error function E is minimised.
Basic Idea:
▶Learn by Iterative Gradient Descent in high-dimensional weight space
▶Pass training data D forward through network, observe error E
▶For each parameter (weight) wi, compute gradient Gwi of error function E
and adjust wi to (wi −η · Gwi), for some learning rate η
Main Problem:
▶How to train the hidden units?
▶Don’t know what their ‘correct’ output should be ⇒cannot calculate error
Solution: Error Backpropagation Algorithm (Rumelhart et al., 1986)
▶Update weights layer by layer, from ‘top’ (output) to ‘bottom’ (input)
▶Estimate error of hidden units proportional to their contribution to the output

chunks.text:
CONVOLUTION
61
Formal definition:
(X ∗ W)[a,b] = ∑i ∑j X[a + i, b + j] W[i, j]
Informal definition:
We take an input tensor, X
and a (usually smaller) kernel, W
and slide W over X, summing

chunks.text:
WHAT TO REMEMBER
●
Deep Learning is a branch of machine learning where the learnable 
function is “deep” = a stack of nonlinear functions
●
Neural Networks are decades old. The main enablers for deep 
learning were faster computers and bigger datasets
(and some practical tweaks that nobody would have found without fast 
computers and large datasets).
●
Promise of deep learning: Less hand-crafting (e.g., of feature 
detectors), less need for domain knowledge
●
Drawback of deep learning: Replaces one design space (feature 
design) with another (network architecture, training data, training 
method); lacks mathematical underpinning
●
Active area of research, scientists still regularly discover new tricks 
and try to improve mathematical understanding

chunks.title:  Descriptive (generative) models
chunks.text:
Motivation
Clustering
Statistical Data Modelling
Supervised vs. Unsupervised Learning
Supervised Learning (= what we will focus on in this class):
▶Input: training set D = {(xi, yi)} of examples xi labeled with class yi ∈Ω
▶Goal: learn classiﬁcation model that predicts class y from features x
 Predictive (discriminative) models
Unsupervised Learning:
▶Input: unlabeled data items D = {(xi)}
▶Goal: learn something about the structure and distribution of the data set
 Descriptive (generative) models
Motivation:
▶Reveal inherent structure in the data
▶Find prototypical cases for characterising data (e.g., for data compression)
▶Find compact descriptive (and perhaps generative) model of given data
▶Compare datasets using such models

chunks.text:
Motivation
Clustering
Statistical Data Modelling
A classical clustering algorithm: k-means
Distance-based Clustering into Disjoint Categories:
The k-means Algorithm
Given:
▶Set of objects D = {xi} ⊂X, i = 1...N
▶Distance measure D(·, ·) in feature space X (e.g., Euclidean distance)
Find:
▶Grouping of the objects into k compact groups (clusters) in such a way that
some quality criterion is optimised
k-means Algorithm:
▶Simple iterative algorithm for ﬁnding a ﬁxed number k of clusters
▶Quality criterion: Mean Quantisation Error
Remarks:
▶Number of clusters k must be speciﬁed by user (parameter)
▶Iterative algorithm with random starting conﬁguration: tries to ﬁnd clustering
with maximum quality, but may get stuck in local optimum

Model Selection via the Bayes Information Criterion (BIC)
Excursus:1
▶The BIC arises from a Bayesian analysis of a model M’s probability, given a
data set D (which we want to maximise):
P(M | D) = P(D | M)P(M)
P(D)
∝P(D | M)P(M) ∝log P(D | M) + log P(M)
Different formulations of the BIC in the literature. One is:
Deﬁnition
The Bayes Information Criterion (BIC) of a model M relative to a data set D is
BIC(M : D) = log P(D | M) −p · log |D|

chunks.title: ▶−log P(D | M) (negative log probability of the data) can be interpreted as
chunks.text:
Motivation
Clustering
Statistical Data Modelling
BIC and the Minimum Message Length Principle
Interpretations of the Bayes Information Criterion (BIC)
BIC(M : D) = log P(D | M) −p · log |D|
2
Overﬁtting Avoidance (‘Regularisation’) Interpretation:
▶BIC trades off the complexity of a model vs. its ﬁt on the data
▶Better ﬁt (high likelihood) is penalised by model complexity (large p)
Alternative (Information-theoretic) Interpretation:
▶−log P(D | M) (negative log probability of the data) can be interpreted as
the number of bits needed to encode the data, given the model
▶p log |D|/2 can be interpreted as the number of bits needed to encode the
model
⇒Maximising BIC = log P(D | M) −p log |D|/2
= minimising (−BIC) = p log |D|/2 −log P(D | M)
= minimising length of message needed to encode model + data (given
the model)
 “Minimum Message Length (MML) Principle”

chunks.text:
Motivation
Clustering
Statistical Data Modelling
BIC and the Minimum Message Length Principle
Applying the BIC to k-means Clustering
Problem:
▶To compute the BIC for a given clustering model M, we need to
- be able to calculate the log-likelihood log P(D | M) of the model
(means: the model must assign probabilities to points in feature space)
- determine the number p of free parameters of M
Solution:
▶View a cluster model as a kind of probability distribution model for which we
know how to calculate P(D | M)
▶Speciﬁcally: view the cluster model as a Gaussian mixture (see below)
▶Calculate log-likelihood log P(D | M) using that model
▶Derive p from that model formulation

chunks.title: GMMs as Density Estimation:
chunks.text:
Motivation
Clustering
Statistical Data Modelling
Relation to Clustering, and to Density Estimation
GMMs, Clustering, and Density Estimation
GMMs as Probabilistic (‘Soft’) Clustering:
▶View k components Ci of GMM as clusters with probabilistic membership
▶Each cluster Ci explicitly described via µi (the cluster center) and Σi
(describes the ‘shape’ of cluster Ci in feature space)
▶From the GMM, we can compute the probabilistic cluster membership
P(Ci | x) (probability with which x belongs to cluster Ci)
GMMs as Density Estimation:
▶By construction, a GMM is a proper density function p(x) over feature space
⇒can use it as a density estimator for p(x | ωi) for classiﬁcation via Bayes’
rule!
▶GMM can generate (sample) new points that obey the same distribution
▶Training algorithm estimates model parameters wi, µi, Σi, but cannot do so
analytically (in contrast to ﬁtting a single Gaussian)

Which of the following sentences correctly reﬂect the underlying reason? The MQE
cannot be used to ﬁnd an ‘optimal’ k∗because
▶it would terminate with k∗= 1 and select a degenerate 1-cluster solution
▶it would select k∗= |D| and select a degenerate 1-example-per-cluster solution
▶it would give the same result for all k and thus be useless for selecting among
different k
▶it can only be computed for those k that are divisors of N = |D|
▶it cannot be compared for different k because the values are on a different scale

Clustering
Statistical Data Modelling
Relation to Clustering, and to Density Estimation
What to expect in the exam: A few typical questions ...
Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs):
1 Given a set D of 100 objects represented in terms of 10 features, how many
parameters (individual numbers) does a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) with k = 3
components have that is deﬁned over this data set?
(Ignore the fact that some of these numbers will be redundant; give the full number of
parameters that will appear in the model.)
2 If we think of this GMM as a (soft) cluster model, how many of these numbers deﬁne
the prototypes (cluster centers)?
3 If we think of this GMM as a (soft) cluster model, what is the meaning of the mixture
coefﬁcients wi? Are they related (proportional) to
▶the degree of typicality of the prototype (centroid) of cluster i
▶the compactness (in terms of expected MQE) of a cluster i
▶the average probability with which objects in D belong to cluster i
▶the expected number of objects in cluster i
4 If we have 1000 instead of 100 objects, we need to estimate
▶1/10 the number of parameters
▶the same number of parameters
▶10 times as many parameters
▶102 times as many parameters
▶102 times as many plus 990 parameters.
55 / 55
